L1857: * * *
L1858: ## 10. Evaluating agentic behaviour【78†¶】
L1859: 
L1860: Everything above is a behaviour you cannot unit-test.
L1861: 
L1862: > ✅ VERIFIED — WWDC26 session 243 (`243:21-26`): "Give a traditional function the same input twice, and you get the same output. LLMs don't work that way… which means standard unit testing breaks down. You can't assert that an output matches a hardcoded string. You have to evaluate the quality and intent of the response instead."
L1863: And Apple's own instruction to do this specifically for the transcript surgery this guide has been recommending:
L1864: 
L1865: > ✅ VERIFIED — `242:185-187`: "When you start to get into nuanced transcript modifications like this, it becomes even more important to use the Evaluations framework to create eval sets and quantify the effect of context engineering strategies. Data driven optimization is the only way to be confident."
L1866: ### 10.1 Why the final answer is not enough【79†¶】
L1867: > ✅ VERIFIED — WWDC26 session 299 (`299:122-124`): "Here's the thing. A model might give you a reasonable-sounding answer without ever calling the right tool. The final output can look correct while the path to get there isn't right."
L1868: >
L1869: > And what a tool evaluation checks (`299:130-133`): "They let you verify the how, not just the what. … The model should call the correct tools, with the correct arguments in the order you expect. And along the way, you'll double check that there weren't any unexpected tool calls in the middle."
L1870: Four checks: correct tools · correct arguments · correct order · no unexpected calls. Map those onto this guide and you get: did the baton get passed · with the right craft · after the user chose · without the sender also trying to write the tutorial itself.
L1871: 
L1872: The memorable framing, which is worth keeping:
L1873: > ✅ VERIFIED — `299:151-152`: "You can think of a trajectory expectation check like going over the list of decisions you made when planning a route. Cars, bikes, and buses are all tools that have their time and place in getting somewhere, but you can evaluate their utility for each segment in a specific trip."
L1874: ### 10.2 The API, as it actually compiles【80†¶】
L1875: 
L1876: Everything in this subsection is ✅ VERIFIED from Apple's Book Tracker sample (`BookTrackerUsingEvaluationsToEvaluateAnIntelligentFeature`, `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET = 27.0`), which ships sixteen trajectory expectations across a 578-line evaluation file.
L1877: 
L1878: > ✅ VERIFIED — `BookTrackerEvaluations/SearchBooks.swift:46-74`, a sample with expectations:
L1879: 
L1880: See the 【160†canonical example】.
L1881: 
L1882: Four `TrajectoryExpectation` initializers, all observed in that one file:
L1883: Form  | Use
L1884: --- | ---
L1885: `TrajectoryExpectation(unordered: [ToolExpectation])`  | presence, order irrelevant
L1886: `TrajectoryExpectation(ordered: [ToolExpectation], allowsAdditionalToolCalls: true)`  | multi-step sequences
L1887: `TrajectoryExpectation(unordered: […], disallowed: [ToolExpectation("findSimilarBooks")])`  | the negative case
L1888: `TrajectoryExpectation(expected: "searchBooks", arguments: […])`  | single-call shorthand
L1889: 
L1890: and the complete argument-matcher vocabulary the sample exercises:
L1891: Matcher  | Example
L1892: --- | ---
L1893: `.exact(argumentName:value:)`  | `.exact(argumentName: "tag", value: .string("gothic"))`
L1894: `.naturalLanguage(argumentName:criteria:)`  | `.naturalLanguage(argumentName: "mood", criteria: "Should relate to uplifting, hopeful, or positive feelings.")`
L1895: `.keyOnly(argumentName:)`  | `.keyOnly(argumentName: "bookId")`
L1896: `.oneOf(argumentName:allowedValues:)`  | `.oneOf(argumentName: "tag", allowedValues: [.string("strategy"), .string("epic")])`
L1897: `.contains(argumentName:substring:)`  | `.contains(argumentName: "tag", substring: "histor")`
L1898: `.hasSuffix(argumentName:suffix:)`  | `.hasSuffix(argumentName: "genre", suffix: "fiction")`
L1899: `.range(argumentName:minimum:maximum:)`  | `.range(argumentName: "limit", minimum: 1, maximum: 3)`
L1900: > `.naturalLanguage` is the headline capability: a model decides whether the argument that was actually passed satisfies a prose criterion. It is how you assert "the craft argument named the thing the user picked" without pinning a string. ✅ 299:163-166: "An exact match isn't always what you want. If the prompt is 'Find something cheerful', the model might pass uplifting, happy, cheerful — any of those are fine.
L1901: The `.naturalLanguage` matcher checks whether the value matches the intent, not the exact string."
L1902: ⚠️ Only `.string(_)` appears as a value wrapper anywhere in the corpus. 🔴 `.number` / `.bool` / `.array` are unverified — and remain so after the 2026-07-29 SDK capture: the wrapper type belongs to the Evaluations framework, whose interface was not captured (no `Evaluations-27.0-macos.swiftinterface` exists in `notes/sdk-interfaces/`).
L1903: One observation worth recording: the shape exactly matches `GeneratedContent.Kind`, whose full case list is SDK-verified (`null` / `bool(Bool)` / `number(Double)` / `string(String)` / `array([GeneratedContent])` / `structure(properties:orderedKeys:)`, `FoundationModels-27.0-macos.swiftinterface:1376-1384`) — if the matcher's value type is that enum, the siblings exist; nothing here proves it is.
L1904: And the wiring, which has one non-obvious requirement:
L1905: 
L1906: > ✅ VERIFIED — `SearchBooks.swift:525-563`:
L1907: 
L1908: See the 【161†canonical example】.
L1909:   * `ToolCallEvaluator(allPass:percentagePass:)` takes two `Metric`s — strict all-or-nothing, and partial credit.
L1910:   * The trajectory reaches the evaluator only via `ModelSubject(value:transcript:)`, and the transcript must be `session.transcript.structuredTranscript`. Pass the plain `Transcript` and the evaluator has nothing to inspect.
L1911:   * You build the session yourself inside `subject(from:)` — and you must build it the same way the feature does. Book Tracker constructs `SystemLanguageModel(guardrails: .permissiveContentTransformations)` in both the app service and the evaluation; construct it differently and you are evaluating a different system.
L1912: ### 10.3 Evaluating a handoff【81†¶】
L1913: Now apply it to §2. A baton-pass has a trajectory, and it is short:
L1914: 
L1915:     `import Evaluations
L1916:     import FoundationModels
L1917:     import Testing
L1918: 
L1919:     let handoffSamples = [
L1920:         // 1. The baton must be passed, with the craft the user named.
L1921:         ModelSample(
L1922:             prompt: "the paper butterfly one, how do I fold it?",
L1923:             expected: TutorialStarted(craft: "paper butterfly"),
L1924:             instructions: BrainstormInstructions.text,
L1925:             expectations: TrajectoryExpectation(unordered: [
L1926:                 ToolExpectation(
L1927:                     "switchToTutorialMode",
L1928:                     arguments: [
L1929:                         .naturalLanguage(
L1930:                             argumentName: "craft",
L1931:                             criteria: "Should name the paper butterfly the person selected."
L1932:                         )
L1933:                     ]
L1934:                 )
L1935:             ])
L1936:         ),
L1937:         // 2. Idle chat must NOT pass the baton. The negative case is the one
L1938:         //    that catches an over-eager handoff, and nothing else will.
L1939:         ModelSample(
L1940:             prompt: "these are all lovely, what do you think of the second one?",
L1941:             expected: StillBrainstorming(),
L1942:             instructions: BrainstormInstructions.text,
L1943:             expectations: TrajectoryExpectation(
L1944:                 unordered: [],
L1945:                 disallowed: [ToolExpectation("switchToTutorialMode")]
L1946:             )
L1947:         ),
L1948:     ]
L1949:     `
L1950: > 🟡 RECONSTRUCTED — the samples. Every type, initializer and matcher used is ✅ verified from Book Tracker (§10.2); the handoff scenario is ours.
L1951: 
L1952: Sample 2 is the important one and it is the one people skip. A baton tool that fires too eagerly is invisible in output quality — the model still answers, just from the wrong persona, with the wrong model, at the wrong temperature, having burned a full prefix invalidation. `disallowed` is the only assertion that catches it.
L1953: ### 10.4 `disallowed` is also your injection test【82†¶】
L1954: > Community framing, and a good one — `coreai-model-zoo/knowledge/evaluations-framework.md`: "299's mechanism for 'the model must not call `findSimilarBooks`' is exactly the gate an agentic security checklist asks for: feed poisoned context, then assert the destructive tool is absent from the trajectory and the parameters weren't rewritten (`naturalLanguage` matcher on the recipient/target). This converts 'we mitigated injection' from a claim into a number you can hill-climb."
L1955: For the patterns in this guide that means: put a hostile string in the tool output your phone-a-friend consultant returns, or in the retrieved document your baton-pass profile inherits, and assert with `disallowed` that no destructive tool appears. It is the only deterministic security test in the stack.
L1956: Relevant to §4.2's third worked call: phone-a-friend's isolation is a mitigation you can now measure. Run the same poisoned-context sample against a shared-transcript design and an isolated- child design, and the difference in trajectory-pass rate is your containment number.
L1957: ### 10.5 What to expect when you run it【83†¶】
L1958: 
L1959: Three findings worth carrying in, all ✅ verified from session 299 and Book Tracker:
L1960:   * Scores drop when the dataset grows, and that is the small set having flattered you. ✅ `299:100-102`: "I've went ahead and ran the evaluation with our new dataset of 100 samples… we're expecting the scores to drop! And we were correct! … Our tag generation feature looked like it was performing well earlier because we weren't testing it with a comprehensive dataset."
L1961:   * Coverage beats count. ✅ `299:40`: "What matters far more than quantity is coverage! So instead of asking how many samples do I need? Ask yourself, have I covered the meaningful variety of ways this feature will actually be used?"
L1962:   * Stamp the prompt into the run record. Book Tracker passes `.evaluates(evaluation, info: ["Prompt": BookTaggingService.instructions, …])` so runs are diffable in Xcode's Compare view. For orchestration work, add the route: which model, which profile, which `toolCallingMode`. Otherwise a regression tells you the number moved and nothing about why.

L1967: ### 11.1 The two patterns【85†¶】
L1968:  | Baton-pass  | Phone-a-friend
L1969: --- | --- | ---
L1970: Apple's word  | collaboration  | consultation
L1971: Tool's side effect  | sets the active-profile variable  | spawns a short-lived child session
L1972: Transcript  | one, shared, fully visible to both  | two, isolated; child's never merges
L1973: Final answer  | the receiving profile  | always the parent
L1974: Cost  | one prefix invalidation per switch  | one child prefill per consultation
L1975: Bound the damage with  | `historyTransform`, switch at boundaries  | `maximumResponseTokens` on the child, validate the return
